title: What everyone knows
objectives: Reason about common knowledge in islander and muddy-children puzzles by induction.

screens.title: Muddy faces
screens.prose: A teacher tells three children: 'At least one of you has a muddy face'. Each sees the others' faces, never her own. Round after round she asks: 'Step forward if you know your face is muddy'. Everyone reasons perfectly and answers honestly.

state.caption: 1 muddy. Each child sees the others, never herself.

frames.caption: 1 muddy. Each child sees the others, never herself.
2 muddy. Each child sees the others, never herself.
3 muddy. Each child sees the others, never herself.

screens.question: In which round do the muddy children step forward?

hints.text: With 1 muddy, what does she see?
She sees no mud, so the teacher's mud must be hers.
With 2 muddy, round 1 is silent, and each then knows she is muddy too: round 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what each silent round tells the children.

byKey.r0c1: One muddy child sees only clean faces, so she knows at once: round 1.
byKey.r1c1: With 2 muddy, each sees one muddy face and waits. Round 1 is silent, so both step forward in round 2.
byKey.r2c1: With 3 muddy, rounds 1 and 2 are silent, so all three step forward in round 3.

explain.text: One muddy child sees no mud and steps forward at once. With two, round 1's silence tells each that the other is not alone: round 2. Three follow in round 3, and so on.

screens.title: Round one is silent
screens.prose: Two muddy children, A and B; C is clean. A sees B muddy and C clean. In round 1 nobody steps forward.

state.caption: A's view: she sees B and C, never herself.

screens.question: What does A conclude after round 1?

options.why: If A were clean, B would see no mud and step forward in round 1. B did not.
The silence is news. B's staying back means B saw mud, and only A can be muddy for B.

hints.text: Suppose A were clean. What would B see?
B would see no muddy face, so B would step forward in round 1.
B stayed back, so A is muddy.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what B would have done if A were clean.

byKey.clean: A clean A leaves B seeing no mud, and B would have stepped forward.
byKey.nothing: B's silence rules out the world where A is clean.

explain.text: If A were clean, B would see no mud and step forward in round 1. B stayed back, so A must be muddy, and she steps forward in round 2. Principle: silence is information when someone would have acted.

screens.title: Seven islanders
screens.prose: Seven islanders all have blue eyes, but nobody knows their own colour. Nobody discusses eye colour, and anyone who learns their eyes are blue must leave that night. A visitor announces: 'I see someone with blue eyes'.

state.caption: Each islander sees six blue-eyed people.

screens.question: On which night do the islanders leave?

hints.text: This is the muddy children with 7 muddy faces.
With $k$ blue-eyed, they leave on night $k$.
Six silent nights, then all seven leave on night 7.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Treat it as 7 muddy children.

byKey.one: Each sees six blue-eyed people, so nobody can be sure on night 1.
byKey.never: The visitor's sentence starts the clock; without it, nobody would leave.
byKey.six: Each sees six, and waits to see whether those six leave on night 6. They do not, so all leave on night 7.

explain.text: With $k$ blue-eyed islanders, each sees $k - 1$ and waits to see if those leave on night $k - 1$. When they do not, all $k$ leave on night $k$. So seven islanders leave together on night 7.

screens.title: Four logicians
screens.prose: Four logicians sit in a café. The waiter asks whether everyone wants a coffee. The first three answer in turn, each saying 'I don't know'. The fourth wants one.

state.caption: Each knows only her own wish.

screens.question: What does the fourth logician say?

options.why: She has heard enough: each 'I don't know' means that person wants one.
Nobody said no, and a logician who did not want one would have said no at once.

hints.text: Why would logician 1 say 'I don't know' rather than 'No'?
She wants one, but cannot speak for the others.
So each 'I don't know' means yes for that person. The fourth wants one too.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decode what each 'I don't know' says about the speaker.

byKey.idk: Each earlier answer shows that speaker wants a coffee. With her own wish, she knows.
byKey.no: Anyone who did not want one would have said no, ending the question.

explain.text: A logician who wanted no coffee would answer no at once. So each 'I don't know' means the speaker wants one. The fourth, wanting one herself, knows everyone does and says yes.

screens.title: Nothing new
screens.prose: Back to the seven blue-eyed islanders. A candidate objects: each islander already saw six blue-eyed people, so the visitor said nothing new.

state.caption: Everyone saw blue eyes before the visitor spoke.

screens.question: When do they leave, and why does the visitor matter?

options.text: Night 7: the sentence became common knowledge
Never: the sentence told nobody anything new
options.why: You checked what each islander knows, not what each knows the others know. The announcement made it common knowledge.

options.text: Night 1: the sentence tells each of them
options.why: Each still sees six blue-eyed people, so nobody can be sure on night 1.

hints.text: With 2 blue-eyed islanders, does each know that the other sees blue eyes?
No: each might be the only one with blue eyes, seen by nobody.
The visitor makes 'someone has blue eyes' known to all, known to be known, and so on.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what each islander knows about what the others know.

byKey.never: Everyone knew the fact, but not that everyone knew that everyone knew it. The visitor supplied that.
byKey.one: Each sees six others with blue eyes, so the sentence is true without them. They need six silent nights.

explain.text: Each islander knew someone had blue eyes, but the chain of 'knows that knows' ran out after six links. The public sentence made the fact common knowledge and started the count. Principle: a public announcement changes what everyone knows that everyone knows.

screens.title: A single islander
screens.prose: Edge case. One islander has blue eyes; the others have brown eyes. The visitor announces: 'I see someone with blue eyes'.
screens.question: On which night does the blue-eyed islander leave?

hints.text: What does he see?
He sees no blue eyes at all.
So the visitor must mean him: he leaves on night 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. He sees no blue eyes, so the sentence is about him.

byKey.never: Here the sentence is real news: he saw no blue eyes before.
byKey.two: He needs no silent night; he sees nobody else with blue eyes.

explain.text: He sees only brown eyes, so the visitor can mean only him. He leaves on night 1. This is the base case of the induction.

screens.title: Silence is news
screens.prose: Each time, $k$ people with the feature waited through $k - 1$ silent rounds, then acted together. The announcement mattered because everyone then knew that everyone knew it: **common knowledge**. $$\text{round} = k$$ The proof is induction on $k$.
screens.question: Eight children are muddy. How many silent rounds pass before they step forward?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. They step forward in round 8, after the silent rounds before it.

byKey.eight: They step forward in round 8, so 7 rounds are silent.
byKey.zero: Each sees 7 muddy faces and must wait to see if those 7 act.

explain.text: Eight muddy children step forward in round 8. Rounds 1 to 7 are silent, each silence ruling out one more world. That is the induction: $k$ muddy act in round $k$.

screens.title: The induction
screens.prose: Order the proof that $k$ muddy children step forward in round $k$. One line does not belong.
screens.question: Order the proof.

lines.text: Base: with 1 muddy child, she sees no mud and steps forward in round 1.
Hypothesis: with $k$ muddy, they step forward in round $k$ and not before.
Step: with $k + 1$ muddy, each muddy child sees $k$ muddy faces.
If she were clean, those $k$ would step forward in round $k$.
Round $k$ is silent, so she is muddy and steps forward in round $k + 1$.
Each child steps forward in the round that equals the muddy faces she sees.
lines.why: With $k$ muddy a muddy child sees $k - 1$ faces, so this rule acts a round early, before she can know.

hints.text: Base case, hypothesis, then the step.
In the step, compare what she sees with the hypothesis.
The silence of round $k$ rules out her being clean.

feedback.correct: Base, hypothesis, what she sees, the world she rules out, the conclusion.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the shape of an induction proof.

byKey.d1: A muddy child sees one face fewer than the number muddy, so she cannot act that early.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the counting rule belongs.

explain.text: The base case is the single muddy child. In the step, a muddy child sees $k$ faces and uses the hypothesis on the world where she is clean. Round $k$'s silence kills that world, so she acts in round $k + 1$.

screens.title: Drill: nine children
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Nine children, five of them muddy. The teacher says that at least one is muddy and asks each round.
screens.question: In which round do the muddy children step forward?

hints.text: Only the muddy count matters.
With $k$ muddy, round $k$.
Five muddy: round 5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With $k$ muddy they step forward in round $k$.

byKey.four: Each muddy child sees 4, but must watch round 4 pass in silence first.
byKey.nine: The clean children do not count.
byKey.one: Each sees muddy faces, so nobody is sure in round 1.

explain.text: Each muddy child sees 4 muddy faces and waits to see if they step forward in round 4. They do not, so all five step forward in round 5. The four clean children never do.

screens.title: Drill: a hundred islanders
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. A hundred islanders have blue eyes, under the island rules. The visitor says: 'I see someone with blue eyes'.
screens.question: On which night do they leave?

hints.text: Same induction, larger $k$.
Each sees 99 blue-eyed people.
They leave on night 100.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With $k$ blue-eyed, night $k$.

byKey.ninetynine: Each sees 99 and waits for night 99 to pass in silence.
byKey.one: Each sees 99 others, so nobody is sure on night 1.

explain.text: Each sees 99 blue-eyed people and waits to see if they leave on night 99. When nobody does, each knows the hundredth is herself. All 100 leave on night 100.

screens.title: Drill: a no
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Three logicians are asked whether everyone wants a coffee. The first says 'I don't know'. The second says 'No'.
screens.question: What does the third say?

options.why: Once anyone says no, the answer is settled for everyone.
The second does not want one, so not everyone does.

hints.text: What does the second logician's 'No' mean?
She does not want a coffee.
Then not everyone wants one, whatever the third wants.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. One 'No' settles the question for the group.

byKey.idk: Her own wish no longer matters. The second's no already decides it.
byKey.yes: Everyone includes the second logician, who said no.

explain.text: The second said no, so she does not want one. Not everyone wants a coffee, so the third says no, whatever she wants. Principle: one counterexample answers an 'everyone' question.

screens.title: At least two
screens.prose: Follow-up. Six children, and the teacher now says: 'At least two of you are muddy'. A widely expected rate cut still matters once announced: it becomes common knowledge among traders.
screens.question: For each number of muddy children, in which round do they step forward?

hints.text: With 2 muddy, each sees exactly one muddy face.
At least two are muddy, so each knows she is the second: round 1.
Each extra muddy child adds one round: round $k - 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The base case is now 2 muddy, who act at once.

byKey.r0c1: Each of the two sees one muddy face. The teacher said at least two, so each is muddy: round 1.
byKey.r1c1: Three muddy: each sees two and waits one round. Round 2.
byKey.r2c1: Four muddy act in round 3, one round sooner than with 'at least one'.

explain.text: With 'at least two', two muddy children each see one face and know at once: round 1. The induction then adds a round per child, so $k$ muddy act in round $k - 1$. Four muddy among six step forward in round 3.

ideas: With $k$ people holding the hidden feature, nobody can act before round $k$; then all $k$ act together.
Each silent round is news: it rules out every world in which someone would have acted.
An announcement everyone already believed still matters: it makes the fact common knowledge.

formula.name: When they act
formula.note: $k$ with the feature, after 'at least $m$' is announced; $m = 1$ gives round $k$.

summary.trap: The visitor said nothing new to anyone, but made it known that everyone knows, so they leave on night 7.

quiz.prose: Six children, four of them muddy. The teacher says that at least three are muddy and asks each round.
quiz.question: In which round do the muddy children step forward?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The base case is now 3 muddy, who act in round 1.

byKey.four: That is the 'at least one' answer.
byKey.one: Each sees three muddy faces, which the teacher's sentence already allows. She must wait a round.
byKey.three: That is the 'at least two' answer.

explain.text: With 'at least three', three muddy children act in round 1. Four muddy each see three and wait one round. They step forward in round 2.

quiz.prose: Two children are muddy, and the teacher never says anything about mud. She still asks each round, 'Step forward if you know your face is muddy.'
quiz.question: Do the muddy children ever step forward?

options.why: Without the announcement, round 1's silence means nothing: each may be clean.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Without the announcement, nothing rules out a world with no mud.

byKey.yes: The round-2 argument needs 'at least one' to be common knowledge.

explain.text: Each sees one muddy face, so each knows someone is muddy. But neither knows the other knows it, so silence proves nothing. Without the announcement they never step forward.

quiz.prose: On the island, a visitor said: 'I see someone with blue eyes'. One islander sees five blue-eyed people. On night 5 nobody leaves.
quiz.question: What does she conclude?

options.text: Her eyes are blue, and she leaves on night 6

options.why: If her eyes were not blue, the five would have left on night 5.

options.text: Nothing yet: she waits for night 7
options.why: Night 5's silence already rules out her being not blue.

feedback.correct: Blue, so she leaves on night 6.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the five would do if she were not blue.

byKey.brown: Five blue-eyed islanders alone would leave on night 5. They did not.
byKey.wait: The silence of night 5 is enough.

explain.text: If her eyes were not blue, the five she sees would leave on night 5. They did not, so there are six blue-eyed islanders including her. All six leave on night 6.
